translations.1799: From Latin cedere, to go or yield. Ced, cede, ceed, and cess are related forms that help explain meanings such as advancing, retreating, process, succession, and yielding.
translations.1800: Start with going or moving, add the directional prefixes to ced, cede, ceed, or cess, and compare each word's actual meaning.
translations.1802: The idea of things following one another gradually extends to outcomes and success.
translations.1851: From Latin specere and spectare, to look or observe, with related forms including spic. Some English spellings and meanings have changed historically.
translations.1852: Inspect suggests looking into; respect historically involves looking back or regarding something; prospect suggests looking forward. These are memory connections.
translations.1880: From Latin portare, to carry or transport. Port meaning harbour has a separate historical route; not every word containing port comes from carrying.
translations.1881: Transport suggests carrying across, export carrying out, and import carrying in.
translations.1905: From tract-, a participial stem of Latin trahere, to pull or drag. The direction of pulling provides a memory connection.
translations.1906: Attract suggests pulling toward oneself; distract pulling attention away; extract pulling something out.
translations.1933: From Latin scribere, to write, and its participial stem script-. Scrib, scribe, and script are related forms.
translations.1934: Describe suggests writing down or describing; transcript relates to writing across; prescribe to writing beforehand.
translations.1957: From Latin struere, to build or arrange; struct- is a related participial stem.
translations.1958: As memory images, construct means building together, instruct suggests organizing understanding, and obstruct suggests building an obstacle in front.
translations.1983: From Latin dicere, to say, and the related stem dict-. Many words suggest saying or declaring something.
translations.1984: Predict suggests saying beforehand; contradict speaking against; dictionary collects words and what they say.
translations.2009: From Latin videre, to see, with forms including vis- and vid-. Some meanings have developed from sight to foresight or judgement.
translations.2010: Visible means able to be seen; revise suggests looking again; supervise suggests watching from above.
translations.2034: From Latin forma, shape or appearance. Think of changing shape, taking form, or conforming to a form.
translations.2035: Transform suggests changing form; reform reshaping; uniform having one consistent form.
translations.2062: From Greek bios, life, common in life-science terms and modern scientific compounds.
translations.2063: Bio plus -logy connects studying life with biology; bio plus -graphy connects recording a life with biography.
translations.2083: From Greek graphein, to write or draw. Graph and -graphy appear in terms for records, images, and fields of study.
translations.2084: Photo-, light, plus graph gives photograph; geo-, earth, plus -graphy gives geography.
translations.2106: From Greek phone, sound, common in sound devices and linguistic terminology.
translations.2107: Tele-, distant, plus phone gives telephone; micro-, small, plus phone helps recall microphone as a sound-pickup device.
translations.2128: From Greek chronos, time, found in many medical, technological, and historical terms.
translations.2129: Chrono-, time, plus -logy gives chronology; syn-, together, in synchronize supplies the idea of matching time.
translations.2150: From Latin credere, to believe or trust. Modern credit also has a background of trust and confidence.
translations.2151: Cred suggests belief: credible means believable; in- reverses that idea in incredible.
translations.2174: From Latin mittere, to send, and the participial stem miss-. Related forms sometimes involve assimilation and spelling changes.
translations.2175: Transmit suggests sending across, submit sending forward for consideration, and permit letting something pass.
translations.2203: From Latin iacere, to throw, and related derivatives of the participial form iactus.
translations.2204: Project suggests throwing forward; reject throwing back; inject putting something into another thing.
translations.2231: From rupt-, the participial stem of Latin rumpere, to break.
translations.2232: Interrupt suggests breaking into something in progress; disrupt disturbing its order; erupt bursting outward.
translations.2256: From Latin ducere, to lead, and the participial stem duct-.
translations.2257: Produce suggests leading forth; reduce leading back; conduct leading together.
translations.2286: From Latin audire, to hear, connected with hearing, audiences, and auditions.
translations.2287: Aud suggests hearing: audible can be heard; an audience is a group assembled to listen.
translations.2303: From Latin vocare, to call, with forms including voc and vok. Their spelling gives a historical clue, not proof that every word is assembled from modern morphemes.
translations.2304: Advocate suggests speaking in support of someone; invoke calling upon; revoke calling back.
translations.2325: From Latin locus, a place, and locare, to place, common in terms about location and allocation.
translations.2326: Relocate means placing in a new location; allocate means assigning to particular places or purposes.
translations.2346: From Latin bene, well or good. English forms such as benef- and benev- often have positive meanings.
translations.2347: Connect benefit with doing good and benevolent with wishing well.
translations.2366: From Greek tele, distant, common in remote communication and observation.
translations.2367: Telephone carries sound over a distance; television carries images over a distance.
translations.2384: From Greek ge or geo, earth or land, found in geography, geology, geothermal, and related words.
translations.2385: Geo plus -graphy describes the earth in geography; geo plus -logy studies it in geology.
translations.2405: From Greek therme, heat, common in physical and medical vocabulary.
translations.2406: Therm plus meter gives an instrument for measuring heat or temperature; geo plus therm points to heat from the earth.
translations.2417: From Latin flectere, to bend. Flex is a related form, and flex or flect often suggests bending or turning.
translations.2418: Reflect suggests bending back; flexible extends the physical ability to bend into adaptability.
translations.2441: From Latin manus, hand, found in words about manual work, manuscripts, and manufacturing.
translations.2442: Manu plus script suggests a handwritten manuscript; manu plus fact connects making by hand with manufacture.
translations.2456: From Latin aqua, water. Aqu- and aqua- occur in words about water, aquatic environments, and water engineering.
translations.2457: Extend aquarium to aquatic and aqueduct, linking their meanings through water.
translations.2477: From Greek phōs and phōt-, light. Photo- is related to the everyday meaning photograph, but its more basic connection is light.
translations.2478: Connect photograph, recording with light, to photosynthesis, using light to produce substances.
translations.2494: From Greek mikros, small. Micro- often means very small and contrasts with macro-, large.
translations.2495: Think of a microscope as a tool for seeing small things, then explore microplastic and microchip.
translations.2515: From Latin multus, many. Multi- is a productive prefix meaning many or multiple.
translations.2516: Remember multilingual, then connect it with multicultural and multinational.
translations.2536: From Greek psychē, life, mind, or soul. Psych- is common in words about psychology and mental activity.
translations.2537: Psychology studies mental processes; psychotherapy refers to psychological treatment. Psychiatry and psychology are not the same field.
translations.2555: From Greek kyklos, circle or wheel, with related words involving cycles, rotation, and reuse.
translations.2556: Ride a bicycle, recognize a cycle, then recycle materials for reuse.
translations.2572: From Greek autos, self. Auto- often means self or automatic.
translations.2573: Compare automatic, autonomous, and autobiography: acting automatically, governing oneself, and writing one's own life.
translations.2591: From Latin terra, land or earth. The terr- family commonly relates to land, regions, or Earth.
translations.2592: Extend territory to terrestrial and extraterrestrial: land, Earth, and beyond Earth.
translations.2613: From Latin lumen, light. Lumin- words emphasize shining, brightness, and illumination.
translations.2614: Connect luminous with illuminate and bioluminescence, the production of light by organisms.
translations.2634: From Greek metron, measure. Meter and metr- often refer to units, measurement, or metrology.
translations.2635: Remember meter as a unit or measuring instrument, then explore kilometer, diameter, and symmetry.
translations.2655: Success is related to Latin successus, progress or outcome. It first emphasized the result of events and later commonly a favourable result, success.
translations.2656: Success is a noun naming achievement. Connect it with succeed, to achieve or take over, and successful, an adjective.
translations.2657: Successful is formed from success and the adjective suffix -ful, meaning achieving success or producing a good result.
translations.2658: Success is a noun; successful is an adjective. The project was successful describes the project's outcome.
translations.2659: Successfully adds the adverb suffix -ly to successful, meaning in a successful or smooth manner.
translations.2660: Successful describes a thing; successfully modifies an action. She successfully completed the task describes how it was completed.
translations.2661: Succeed goes back to Latin succedere, to come after or take over. It also developed the common sense of achieving a goal.
translations.2662: Compare succeed in doing something, achieve it, with succeed someone, take over that person's position.
translations.2663: Successor belongs to the succeed family and names someone taking over another person's position or status.
translations.2664: A successor is the person who follows in a position; compare predecessor, the previous holder.
translations.2665: Succession is related to succeed and successor and emphasizes one following another, including a sequence or inheritance of a position.
translations.2666: A succession of events is a series of events; a succession plan prepares for someone to take over a role.
translations.2667: Successive belongs to the sequence-related branch of succession and describes things occurring one immediately after another.
translations.2668: Successive days are consecutive days. Do not confuse successive with successful.
translations.2669: Process is related to Latin processus, advancement or going forward, and developed senses of development and step-by-step activity.
translations.2670: Process emphasizes an activity unfolding, as in a learning process or manufacturing process.
translations.2671: Proceed comes from Latin procedere, to go forward, combining pro-, forward, with cedere, to go. It commonly means continuing.
translations.2672: Proceed with the plan means continue carrying it out. Connect pro- with forward and ced or ceed with going.
translations.2673: Procedure entered English through French procédure, related to procéder and Latin procedere, to proceed. Pro-, forward, ced, going, and the noun ending -ure provide a learning analysis of a prescribed method or procedure.
translations.2674: Imagine completing a task step by step. The prescribed sequence is a procedure.
translations.2675: Procession is related to Latin processio, going forward, and commonly names an organized line of people moving forward.
translations.2676: A procession emphasizes people advancing in a line, as in a wedding procession.
translations.2677: Access is related to Latin accedere, to approach, and developed senses of entry, reaching, and the right to use something.
translations.2678: Access to information is the ability or means to obtain it. Have access to means being able to enter or use something.
translations.2679: Accessible belongs to the access family and describes something reachable, obtainable, or easy to understand.
translations.2680: An accessible website is easy to access; an accessible explanation is easy to understand.
translations.2681: Recede comes from Latin recedere, to go back or withdraw. Re- suggests back and ced or cede going.
translations.2682: Recede can describe retreating water, a moving-back hairline, or something growing more distant.
translations.2683: Recession is related to Latin recessio, retreat or withdrawal. In modern economics it describes a decline in economic activity.
translations.2684: An economic recession is an economic downturn. Connect it with recede, to move back.
translations.2685: Concede is related to Latin concedere, to yield, grant, or agree, and commonly means acknowledging a point or giving way.
translations.2686: Concede a point means acknowledge it; concede defeat means admit that one has lost.
translations.2687: Concession belongs to the yielding or granting family of concede. It can mean a compromise, a special allowance, or an operating right.
translations.2688: Make a concession means yield a point or condition. A concession agreement may grant operating rights.
translations.2689: Precede comes from Latin praecedere, to go before, combining prae-, before, and cedere, to go. It commonly means happening before something else.
translations.2690: A precedes B means A comes before B. Precedence is the related noun for priority or coming first.
translations.2691: Precedent is related to precede and names an earlier example that can guide later events, including in law.
translations.2692: Set a precedent means establish a prior example. A legal precedent is an earlier legal decision used as guidance.
translations.2693: Excess is related to Latin excedere, to go beyond a boundary, and means an amount beyond a normal or proper limit.
translations.2694: In excess of means more than; excess capacity means capacity beyond what is needed.
translations.2695: Excessive is formed from excess and the adjective suffix -ive, meaning beyond a reasonable limit.
translations.2696: Excessive spending and excessive pressure both describe amounts beyond what is normal or appropriate.
